summary: MARS Pathfinder is a browser-based Mars map and expedition planner built on open NASA and USGS data. It answers one practical question: "Can a crew get from A to B on Mars safely, and what will they need?" Users draw a route or let the planner find one; every stretch is checked against HiRISE/CTX/MOLA elevation for slope, loose ground and missing data. For an astronaut on foot or a rover, it computes oxygen, water, food, EVA time and the way back to the nearest base, and treats bases along the route as resupply stops. A Mars clock drives modelled temperature, UV and radiation dose (scaled from Curiosity RAD), which can be played along the route. Twelve thematic science views (gravity, minerals, magnetics, geology, seismic and more), a 3D globe, HiRISE terrain cut-outs, rover raw images and a knowledge base complete the tool. Every value is labelled as measured, derived/model or assumption – nothing is invented, and the app needs no API keys.
details: WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS MARS Pathfinder is a browser-based Mars map and expedition planner. It answers one practical question for future crewed missions: "Can a crew get from A to B on Mars safely, and what will they need?" - Map: NASA Mars Trek imagery (Viking, MOLA, THEMIS, CTX, HiRISE) combined with USGS high-resolution elevation models (HiRISE ≈1 m, CTX 20 m, MOLA 463 m as global fallback), read directly as Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs and found through the USGS STAC catalogue. - Route planning: the user sets point A and B and either draws a route or lets the planner search the safest one. A coarse corridor on MOLA is refined on a fine grid checked against every elevation pixel. It avoids slopes above the chosen limit, loose ground (THEMIS night-IR thermal inertia) and areas without data, and re-plans around unsafe spots. - Crew or vehicle: for an astronaut on foot or a rover (Curiosity, Perseverance, pressurized rover presets) it computes walking energy (Pandolf equation scaled to Mars gravity), oxygen, water, food, toilet capacity, EVA time, range and seats. Bases near the route are recognised as resupply stops, so a trip can be split into legs: go to a base, refill, continue or return. - Environment: a Mars clock (NASA GISS Mars24 algorithm) drives modelled surface temperature (heat-conduction model driven by TES thermal inertia and albedo), UV and cosmic-radiation dose (scaled from Curiosity RAD measurements at Gale by atmospheric column depth) plus soil gamma dose from Odyssey GRS potassium and thorium. All of this can be replayed along the route as a "route walk" next to the elevation profile. - Science views: 12 thematic layers – MRO gravity (GMM-3), crustal thickness, crustal magnetic field, GRS elements (Fe, Si, Cl, H2O, K, Th), TES minerals, USGS geologic map, valley networks, InSight seismic sources and more. - Extras: 3D globe, 3D terrain cut-outs from HiRISE DTMs, live rover raw images that can be annotated, Mars weather, and a knowledge base explaining NASA findings with photos and a "safe / maybe / not safe" rating of how well each statement is established. A step-by-step tutorial helps first-time users. BENEFITS - One tool instead of dozens of separate datasets and portals: map, terrain, route, logistics and environment in one place. - It shows not only where you can go, but what it costs (oxygen, water, food, time, radiation dose) and where you need a base. - Data honesty: every value is labelled as measured (NASA/USGS data), derived/model (computed with a documented model) or assumption (a planning value with a stated reason). Nothing is invented. A full data audit with all sources is in the repository. - Runs in any browser, free, no installation, no API keys. INTENDED IMPACT - Help students, educators and space enthusiasts understand what a real Mars expedition involves – terrain, life support and radiation – using real mission data. - Give a first-order planning tool for thinking about landing-site traverses, base placement and resupply. - Make NASA's open Mars data more accessible and show how different datasets connect. TOOLS, LANGUAGES, SOFTWARE - JavaScript, HTML, CSS (no build step); Leaflet (2D map), three.js (3D globe and terrain), geotiff.js (reading elevation models in the browser). - Python (standard library only) for a local server and for preparing the science grids. - NASA APIs and services: Mars Trek WMTS, USGS STAC / Astrogeology DTMs, Mars rover raw images, Mars weather and rover waypoint data, PDS datasets. - GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting; DaVinci Resolve for the video. - No special hardware – developed on a normal laptop. - AI assistance: we used Claude (Anthropic) as a coding assistant during development. The app itself uses no AI at runtime. CREATIVITY - It treats Mars not as a picture but as a place to travel: you plan a walk, then "walk" it in time and see temperature, radiation and supplies change along the way. - Resupply logic: the planner understands that a crew can stop at another base, refill and continue – not just "too far, impossible". - Every number tells you where it comes from, which is rare in maps and games. FACTORS WE CONSIDERED - Scientific accuracy: real NASA/USGS data only; models documented with references; validity ranges noted (e.g. radiation scaling only valid for a certain atmospheric column depth). - Safety margins: slope and tip-over limits, reserve oxygen and food, the way back to base. - Usability: bilingual interface (English/German), tutorial, info pages with photos for every layer. - Data gaps: high-resolution terrain exists only in some places, so the app falls back to MOLA and warns the user. - Licensing: only public-domain NASA images and open data, all credited.
